newsitem.title: CHINA: China winks at rules, causing B share run-brokers.
newsitem.headline: China winks at rules, causing B share run-brokers.

text.p: A three-week bull run on China's B share markets has been caused primarily by Chinese authorities ignoring their own rules and implicity allowing domestic investors to buy B shares, brokers said on Thursday.

Brokers said the authorities learned a lesson when they ordered Chinese investors to sell their holdings in the foreign-currency B share markets in September, prompting a sharp fall in the B share indices.
The order was aimed at reducing domestic investors' exposure to the inflows and outflows of foreign investors, for whom the B share markets were originally set up, analysts said at the time.

But B shares began to take off again in mid-November, first in Shenzhen and later in Shanghai, after persistent rumours circulated that Beijing planned measures to boost B shares, including allowing Chinese investors to stay in the market.

One Chinese trader said that after the B index hit record lows securities authorities held meetings on how to boost the market and decided that Chinese citizens would quietly be allowed to continue to trade B shares.
"This policy support is the major reason behind the recent rises," he said.

"Beijing realised that you cannot get Chinese investors out of the market without reducing liquidity to the point that the B share market would no longer function," said Bruce Richardson, chief representative of HG Asia Limited in Shanghai.
He said investors saw B shares as undervalued by as much as five times compared with A shares issued by the same company, and expected that the two would eventually be merged.
The Shanghai B share index closed on Thursday at 64.191 points, down 0.941 points on the day on a technical correction, but up 43 percent from a record low of 44.803 points on November 11.
The Shenzhen B share index closed at 172.25, up 4.53 percent on the day and up 94 percent since November 11.

Brokers said the bull run started with buying by local investors, with foreigners joining later. Foreigners came into the market when they saw its sharp rise and a surge in Chinese shares on the Hong Kong market.
"This is a liquidity and sentiment-driven market," said Richard Graham, head of ING Barings in China.

"There has been a wave of liquidity going into Red Chips (Hong Kong-listed companies with major China business interests), some of whose P/Es (price-earnings ratios) are pretty high, up to 30," he said.
"B and H shares inevitably looked cheap by comparison, although the fundamentals (of the companies) and their earnings potential have not really changed," he said.

Chinese traders said another factor for the rise was the belief of many investors that an overall improvement in China's economy this year would help listed companies to improve their performances next year.

"In the recent upsurge, in general, foreigners have been buying the market, not the company," Richardson said. "Although China's economy is clearly turning up, this has not yet raised sales or corporate incomes."
Poor company results were a major reason for B shares falling into a depression from mid-1994, analysts said.
